title: Shooting Stars From Halley's Comet Light Up the Autumn Sky
summary:
Halley's Comet is more than 3 billion miles (4.8 billion kilometers) from Earth right now, but pieces it left behind are still putting on a show. On October 21, astrophotographer Tim McCollum captured three bright Orionid meteors streaking across the sky above Toccoa, Georgia.

The Orionid meteor shower happens each autumn, when Earth passes through the trail of dust and debris shed by Halley's Comet. As the tiny particles burn up in our atmosphere, they become shooting stars. In McCollum's picture, the meteors appear to race away from a point near Betelgeuse, the red giant star in the constellation Orion. That point is called the radiant.

Catching a shooting star on camera takes skill, luck and patience. McCollum photographed the sky between 3 and 4 a.m. using a Canon camera on a star tracker, taking many 30-second exposures. He then combined them into one composite image with astrophoto software.

The finished picture holds more than meteors. The familiar stars of Orion's Belt shine near the glow of the Orion Nebula, one of the closest major star-forming regions to Earth. The Rosette Nebula also appears, tucked into the dense star fields and dust lanes of the Milky Way, which cuts diagonally across the image.

The Orionid shower stays active until November 7, so skywatchers still have chances to spot one of Halley's shooting stars on the next few clear nights. Earth is also passing through debris from Comet 2P/Encke, so a lucky viewer might even catch a bright Taurid meteor, sometimes nicknamed a Halloween Fireball.
why_it_matters: Meteor showers let anyone watching the sky see Earth's journey through a comet's debris trail with their own eyes. This shower stays active until November 7, so families still have clear nights to look for one.

background_read: A comet sheds dust and small pieces as it travels, leaving a trail of debris behind it in space.
When Earth passes through that trail, the tiny pieces burn up in the atmosphere as meteors, which people call shooting stars.
The Orionid meteors seem to come from near the constellation Orion, which is why the shower is named for Orion.
